chapters.title: The witness
chapters.gist: Janaka asks how to know, how to be free and how to let go, and Ashtavakra answers that he is already the free witness of everything.
chapters.speaker: ashtavakra

chapters.title: Janaka's wonder
chapters.gist: Janaka finds himself as awareness and bows to it in astonishment, testing the new view against the world, the body and the crowd.
chapters.speaker: janaka

chapters.title: The test
chapters.gist: Ashtavakra tests the king: if you know the Self, why do greed, desire and fear of freedom still move you?
chapters.speaker: ashtavakra

chapters.title: The knower at play
chapters.gist: The one who knows the Self lives freely, untouched by merit and sin as space is untouched by smoke.
chapters.speaker: janaka

chapters.title: Four ways to rest
chapters.gist: Four short verses, each ending with the same instruction: let the sense of separation dissolve, and rest.
chapters.speaker: ashtavakra

chapters.title: Space, ocean, shell
chapters.gist: Janaka answers that there is nothing to give up, take or dissolve, because the world was never apart from him.
chapters.speaker: janaka

chapters.title: The ship on the ocean
chapters.gist: Janaka watches the world drift like a ship on the ocean of awareness, and feels no need to steer it.
chapters.speaker: janaka

chapters.title: Bondage and freedom
chapters.gist: Four verses that define bondage as the mind wanting and grieving, and freedom as its rest.
chapters.speaker: ashtavakra

chapters.title: Weariness with the world
chapters.gist: Seeing how the opposites never end, one grows tired of chasing them and lets go of every vow.
chapters.speaker: ashtavakra

chapters.title: Quiet
chapters.gist: Leave desire, wealth and even merit; craving is the only bond, and ending it is freedom.
chapters.speaker: ashtavakra

chapters.title: Eight certainties
chapters.gist: Eight verses, each about one who is certain of a single truth and is at peace because of it.
chapters.speaker: ashtavakra

chapters.title: How I came to rest
chapters.gist: Janaka describes how body, speech and thought fell quiet one after another, and how he now rests as he is.
chapters.speaker: janaka

chapters.title: As it pleases me
chapters.gist: Janaka lives without taking or giving up, doing what comes and living at ease.
chapters.speaker: janaka

chapters.title: Peace
chapters.gist: With craving melted, wealth, friends, scripture and learning lose their hold; only those in this state know it.
chapters.speaker: janaka

chapters.title: What you are
chapters.gist: Ashtavakra's second long teaching: you are awareness, the world is waves on your ocean, so move about at ease.
chapters.speaker: ashtavakra

chapters.title: Forget it all
chapters.gist: No scripture or practice brings ease until everything learned is forgotten and effort drops away.
chapters.speaker: ashtavakra

chapters.title: The one who knows
chapters.gist: A portrait of the free person, who wants neither pleasure nor freedom and lives at ease seeing, hearing and eating.
chapters.speaker: ashtavakra

chapters.title: Peace in a hundred verses
chapters.gist: The longest chapter, a third of the text, contrasting the confused who strive with the steady who are already at rest.
chapters.speaker: ashtavakra

chapters.title: My own greatness
chapters.gist: Janaka has pulled the thorn of opinions from his heart; time, place, life and death have no hold on him.
chapters.speaker: janaka

chapters.title: Free while living
chapters.gist: Janaka's last words: in his own nature there is no world, no one seeking freedom, no teacher and no teaching, and nothing rises.
chapters.speaker: janaka

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: कथं ज्ञानमवाप्नोति कथं मुक्तिर्भविष्यति । वैराग्यं च कथं प्राप्तमेतद् ब्रूहि मम प्रभो ॥
verses.iast: kathaṃ jñānamavāpnoti kathaṃ muktirbhaviṣyati | vairāgyaṃ ca kathaṃ prāptametad brūhi mama prabho ||
verses.en: How does one come to know? How does freedom come about? And how is dispassion reached? Tell me this, my lord.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.1 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). King Janaka asks it of his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "How does one come to know? How does freedom come about? And how is dispassion reached? Tell me this, my lord."
verses.notice: Janaka asks three things at once, and the whole text answers them in one stroke.
verses.commentary: The text opens with a king asking a young teacher three plain questions. Janaka of Mithila already has everything a person can want, and tradition links this conversation to the Mahabharata story in which the boy Ashtavakra wins a debate at Janaka's court. So the questions come from someone who has tried the usual answers. He asks about knowledge, freedom and dispassion as if they were separate goals with separate methods. The traditional reading is that Ashtavakra answers all three at once. From the next verse on he treats the three as one fact seen from three sides: when you know what you are, you are free, and craving loses its grip on its own. That is why the Ashtavakra Gita feels so short on instructions. It skips the ladder. Commentators in the Advaita line read Janaka here as the ideal student described in the Upanishads: mature, dispassionate already, and ready to hear the conclusion first. For a reader today, the useful part is the honesty of the question. His question is about what is true, more than about how to feel better.

bridge.note: Krishna tells Arjuna to learn from those who have seen the truth by asking them, and serving them.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: मुक्तिमिच्छसि चेत्तात विषयान् विषवत्त्यज । क्षमार्जवदयातोषसत्यं पीयूषवद् भज ॥
verses.iast: muktimicchasi cettāta viṣayān viṣavattyaja | kṣamārjavadayātoṣasatyaṃ pīyūṣavad bhaja ||
verses.en: If you want freedom, my child, leave the objects of the senses as you would leave poison. Take forgiveness, honesty, kindness, contentment and truth as you would take nectar.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.2 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "If you want freedom, my child, leave the objects of the senses as you would leave poison. Take forgiveness, honesty, kindness, contentment and truth as you would take nectar."
verses.notice: The teacher's first answer is about conduct, before any talk of awareness.
verses.commentary: Ashtavakra calls the king tāta, the word a father uses for a child. Before he says anything about the Self, he gives an ethical instruction. Sense objects are to be left like poison, and five qualities are to be taken like nectar: forgiveness, honesty, kindness, contentment and truth. The image is precise. You do not argue with poison. You leave it in the cup. Nectar you drink. Traditional commentators note that the verse sets the ground for everything that follows. The later chapters say there is nothing to practise and nothing to give up, and readers who skip this verse sometimes take that as permission to drop ordinary decency. The Advaita tradition reads it the other way: a mind that keeps these five qualities becomes quiet enough to hear the teaching in 1.3 onward. Notice how ordinary the list is. Nothing exotic, nothing secret. Forgiveness and contentment are things you can practise at a family dinner or a difficult meeting today, and they are named here as the first step toward freedom.

bridge.note: Krishna's list of the qualities of a gentle nature includes truth, kindness and freedom from greed.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: न पृथ्वी न जलं नाग्निर्न वायुर्द्यौर्न वा भवान् । एषां साक्षिणमात्मानं चिद्रूपं विद्धि मुक्तये ॥
verses.iast: na pṛthvī na jalaṃ nāgnirna vāyurdyaurna vā bhavān | eṣāṃ sākṣiṇamātmānaṃ cidrūpaṃ viddhi muktaye ||
verses.en: You are not earth, water, fire, air or space. To be free, know yourself as the witness of all these, made of awareness.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.3 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "You are not earth, water, fire, air or space. To be free, know yourself as the witness of all these, made of awareness."
verses.notice: Every element is named and set aside, and what remains is the one who sees them.
verses.commentary: Indian philosophy describes the body and the physical world as built from five elements: earth, water, fire, air and space. Ashtavakra lists all five and says you are none of them. This is the method the Upanishads call neti neti, not this, not this. You remove what can be seen until only the seer is left. The key word is sākṣin, the witness. A witness in a court watches events without taking part in them, and that is the sense here. The Advaita teachers point out that whatever you can observe, including your body, your moods and your thoughts, stands in front of you as an object. The one observing cannot be one of those objects. The verse then adds cidrūpa, whose form is awareness, so the witness has content of its own: the plain fact of being aware. Ashtavakra presents this as the means to freedom, muktaye. He asks Janaka to notice what was always the case, with nothing new to believe.

bridge.note: Krishna calls the body the field and the one who knows it the knower of the field.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: यदि देहं पृथक् कृत्य चिति विश्राम्य तिष्ठसि । अधुनैव सुखी शान्तो बन्धमुक्तो भविष्यसि ॥
verses.iast: yadi dehaṃ pṛthak kṛtya citi viśrāmya tiṣṭhasi | adhunaiva sukhī śānto bandhamukto bhaviṣyasi ||
verses.en: If you set the body apart and rest in awareness, you will be happy, at peace and free of bondage this very moment.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.4 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "If you set the body apart and rest in awareness, you will be happy, at peace and free of bondage this very moment."
verses.notice: The verse promises freedom now, adhunā eva, with no waiting period.
verses.commentary: Two actions are named: set the body apart, and rest in awareness. Neither is a physical act. Setting the body apart means seeing it as something you have and use, the way you have a coat, instead of the thing you are. Resting in awareness means letting attention settle on the fact of being aware instead of running after each object. Then comes the startling phrase adhunā eva, right now. Most paths in the tradition speak of gradual purification over years or lifetimes. The Ashtavakra Gita, read by the Advaita teachers, says that freedom is the nature of the Self and so it cannot arrive later. It can only be recognised. The three results listed, happy, peaceful and unbound, are the same three things Janaka asked about in 1.1, in a different order. A reader trying this does not need a retreat. It can be done in a waiting room. Notice the body sitting there, notice that you are aware of it, and stay with the noticing for a few breaths.

bridge.note: Krishna describes the happiness found within by one who is not attached to outer contacts.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: न त्वं विप्रादिको वर्णो नाश्रमी नाक्षगोचरः । असङ्गोऽसि निराकारो विश्वसाक्षी सुखी भव ॥
verses.iast: na tvaṃ viprādiko varṇo nāśramī nākṣagocaraḥ | asaṅgo'si nirākāro viśvasākṣī sukhī bhava ||
verses.en: You are not a Brahmin or of any other varna, you belong to no stage of life, and you are nothing the eyes can see. Unattached and formless, you are the witness of everything. Be happy.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.5 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "You are not a Brahmin or of any other varna, you belong to no stage of life, and you are nothing the eyes can see. Unattached and formless, you are the witness of everything. Be happy."
verses.notice: Caste, stage of life and visible form are all named as things you are not.

words.m: one in a stage of life
within reach of the eyes and senses

verses.commentary: The phrase vipra-ādiko varṇaḥ means a Brahmin or any of the other varnas. Ashtavakra is speaking to a Kshatriya king and tells him he is no varna at all. He adds that Janaka belongs to no āśrama, the four stages of student, householder, forest-dweller and renunciant, and that he is nothing the senses can grasp. These were the main ways a person was placed in society, and all of them belong to the body and its roles. The Advaita reading is consistent: such identities are real for social life and duty, and the Self they describe is untouched by them. The verse leaves dharma in place and says what you are underneath it. The teacher's own name sharpens the point. Ashtavakra means bent in eight places, and in the Mahabharata he is born with a body bent by his father's curse. Here that teacher tells a king that the body is not the person. The verse ends, as many do in this chapter, with a simple instruction: be happy.

bridge.note: Krishna says the wise see the same Self in a learned Brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: धर्माधर्मौ सुखं दुःखं मानसानि न ते विभो । न कर्तासि न भोक्तासि मुक्त एवासि सर्वदा ॥
verses.iast: dharmādharmau sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ mānasāni na te vibho | na kartāsi na bhoktāsi mukta evāsi sarvadā ||
verses.en: Right and wrong, pleasure and pain belong to the mind. They are not yours, all-pervading one. You are not the doer and not the one who enjoys. You are free, always.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.6 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "Right and wrong, pleasure and pain belong to the mind. They are not yours, all-pervading one. You are not the doer and not the one who enjoys. You are free, always."
verses.notice: Right and wrong are moved into the mind, along with pleasure and pain.

words.m: right and wrong, merit and demerit
enjoyer, the one who experiences results

verses.commentary: This verse sounds dangerous until you read it with the tradition. Dharma and adharma here mean merit and demerit, the moral weight that actions leave behind. Ashtavakra places them in the mind along with pleasure and pain. He calls Janaka vibhu, all-pervading, and says the Self is neither the doer of actions nor the one who reaps their results. Advaita teachers are careful with this. The body and mind still act, and they still answer for what they do. Ethics stays in force at the level where action happens. What changes is the sense of who is acting. The Self is compared to light in a room: everything in the room is seen by it, and none of it belongs to it. The phrase mukta eva asi sarvadā, you are always free, is the heart of the verse. Freedom is described as a fact about you, present before any effort, which is why the next verses can say that the only bondage is a mistake about who you are.

bridge.note: Krishna says the Self, though dwelling in the body, does not act and is not stained.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: एको द्रष्टासि सर्वस्य मुक्तप्रायोऽसि सर्वदा । अयमेव हि ते बन्धो द्रष्टारं पश्यसीतरम् ॥
verses.iast: eko draṣṭāsi sarvasya muktaprāyo'si sarvadā | ayameva hi te bandho draṣṭāraṃ paśyasītaram ||
verses.en: You are the one seer of all, and you have always been free. Your only bondage is this: you see the seer as someone else.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.7 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "You are the one seer of all, and you have always been free. Your only bondage is this: you see the seer as someone else."
verses.notice: Bondage is defined as one small error of seeing.

words.m: free in effect, as good as free

verses.commentary: Ashtavakra gives a definition of bondage that fits in half a line: you see the seer as someone other than yourself. In daily life we treat awareness as a property of a small person located behind the eyes. That person then seems to be one object among others, limited and exposed. The verse says this picture is the whole problem. There is one seer of everything, and it is what you are. The word mukta-prāya is unusual. Some commentators read it as free already, since prāya can mean in effect. Others read it as nearly free, meaning that the only thing between Janaka and freedom is this misreading. Both readings agree on the practical point. Nothing has to be built. One mistake has to be dropped. The Advaita teachers compare it to a man looking everywhere for a necklace he is wearing. When a friend points to his neck, he gains nothing new, and he stops searching. The verse invites the same kind of looking.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: अहं कर्तेत्यहंमानमहाकृष्णाहिदंशितः । नाहं कर्तेति विश्वासामृतं पीत्वा सुखी भव ॥
verses.iast: ahaṃ kartetyahaṃmānamahākṛṣṇāhidaṃśitaḥ | nāhaṃ karteti viśvāsāmṛtaṃ pītvā sukhī bhava ||
verses.en: You have been bitten by the great black snake of the thought 'I am the doer'. Drink the nectar of trust in 'I am not the doer', and be happy.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.8 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "You have been bitten by the great black snake of the thought 'I am the doer'. Drink the nectar of trust in 'I am not the doer', and be happy."
verses.notice: The thought 'I am the doer' is a snakebite, and the cure is something you drink.
verses.commentary: A snakebite was the classic emergency in old India, and the black cobra the deadliest snake. Ashtavakra uses that picture for ahaṅkāra, the conviction that I am the one doing everything. The poison works slowly. Every success becomes my success, every failure my failure, and the mind is never at rest. The antidote is named viśvāsa, which means trust or firm conviction. It is the thought 'I am not the doer', held until it becomes natural. The Advaita commentators link this with the Bhagavad Gita, where actions are said to be done by the qualities of nature while the confused self thinks it is the doer. Passivity is not the aim. Work still gets done, often better, because the worker is not carrying the weight of being its only cause. Someone who has prepared well for an interview, and then lets the outcome be, knows a small version of this. The verse asks for that ease to be extended to everything.

bridge.note: Krishna says actions are done by nature's qualities, and the one confused by ego thinks 'I am the doer'.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: एको विशुद्धबोधोऽहमिति निश्चयवह्निना । प्रज्वाल्याज्ञानगहनं वीतशोकः सुखी भव ॥
verses.iast: eko viśuddhabodho'hamiti niścayavahninā | prajvālyājñānagahanaṃ vītaśokaḥ sukhī bhava ||
verses.en: 'I am the one pure awareness': let this certainty be a fire that burns down the forest of not knowing. Then be free of grief, and be happy.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.9 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "'I am the one pure awareness': let this certainty be a fire that burns down the forest of not knowing. Then be free of grief, and be happy."
verses.notice: Certainty is the fire, and ignorance is a whole forest, not a single tree.
verses.commentary: Ignorance here is called gahana, a dense forest, the kind that is easy to get lost in and impossible to clear by hand. A fire clears it in one sweep. The fire is niścaya, a settled certainty: I am the one pure awareness. The tradition distinguishes between knowing something as information and knowing it with certainty. You can hear many times that you are awareness and still live as a frightened body. Niścaya is the point where the knowledge stops being an idea and becomes how you see. Advaita teachers say this certainty comes through hearing the teaching, reflecting on it until doubts are gone, and dwelling on it. Ashtavakra compresses all three into one image. The result named is vīta-śoka, free of grief. Grief is mentioned because it is the feeling that most tightly binds a person to the idea of being a limited self who can lose things. Burn the forest, and grief has nowhere to grow. The word niścaya returns many times in chapter 11.

bridge.note: Krishna says the fire of knowledge burns all actions to ash, as a blazing fire burns firewood.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: यत्र विश्वमिदं भाति कल्पितं रज्जुसर्पवत् । आनन्दपरमानन्दः स बोधस्त्वं सुखं भव ॥
verses.iast: yatra viśvamidaṃ bhāti kalpitaṃ rajjusarpavat | ānandaparamānandaḥ sa bodhastvaṃ sukhaṃ bhava ||
verses.en: That in which this world appears, imagined like a snake on a rope, that joy beyond joy, that awareness: you are that. Be happy.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.10 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "That in which this world appears, imagined like a snake on a rope, that joy beyond joy, that awareness: you are that. Be happy."
verses.notice: The world is compared to a snake seen on a rope, and the rope is you.

words.m: like a snake on a rope

verses.commentary: The rope and the snake is the most famous example in Advaita. In dim light a coiled rope looks like a snake. The fear is real, the heartbeat is real, but nothing is there except rope. When a lamp is brought, the snake does not go anywhere. It was never there. Ashtavakra applies this to the world: it appears in awareness as the snake appears on the rope. The commentators are careful about what this claims. It allows the world its place in daily life and says that it has no being apart from the awareness in which it appears. The second half turns from the world to the reader. That awareness is ānanda, joy, and paramānanda, the highest joy, and you are it. So the instruction to be happy is less a command than a reminder. The verse pairs a large claim about the world with a personal one, and leaves the reader to notice that they are the same claim.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: मुक्ताभिमानी मुक्तो हि बद्धो बद्धाभिमान्यपि । किंवदन्तीह सत्येयं या मतिः सा गतिर्भवेत् ॥
verses.iast: muktābhimānī mukto hi baddho baddhābhimānyapi | kiṃvadantīha satyeyaṃ yā matiḥ sā gatirbhavet ||
verses.en: One who thinks 'I am free' is free. One who thinks 'I am bound' stays bound. The old saying is true: as you hold yourself, so you become.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.11 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "One who thinks 'I am free' is free. One who thinks 'I am bound' stays bound. The old saying is true: as you hold yourself, so you become."
verses.notice: The famous line yā matiḥ sā gatiḥ is quoted as a saying the listener already knows.

words.m: one who holds himself to be free
one who holds himself to be bound
that is the outcome, the destination

verses.commentary: This is the line most people quote from the Ashtavakra Gita, often without knowing its source. Ashtavakra presents the final phrase as a kiṃvadantī, a common saying, and says that here it holds true: yā matiḥ sā gatir bhavet, as your conviction, so your end. The first half applies it. One who takes himself to be free is free, and one who takes himself to be bound stays bound. Read quickly, this sounds like positive thinking. The tradition reads it more carefully. Mati here means the settled view of what you are, something deeper than a mood or an affirmation. Since the Self is already free, according to the previous verses, the only thing keeping a person bound is the view that he is bound. Change the view at its root and nothing else needs to change. Advaita teachers also use the verse as a warning. A person who keeps rehearsing his limitations, his failures and his bad luck builds a gati out of that mati. Where you settle your mind is where you end up living.

bridge.note: Krishna says a person is made of his faith: as one's faith is, so one is.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: आत्मा साक्षी विभुः पूर्ण एको मुक्तश्चिदक्रियः । असङ्गो निःस्पृहः शान्तो भ्रमात्संसारवानिव ॥
verses.iast: ātmā sākṣī vibhuḥ pūrṇa eko muktaścidakriyaḥ | asaṅgo niḥspṛhaḥ śānto bhramātsaṃsāravāniva ||
verses.en: The Self is the witness: all-pervading, whole, one, free, awareness itself, without action, unattached, without wanting, at peace. Only through error does it seem caught in worldly life.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.12 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "The Self is the witness: all-pervading, whole, one, free, awareness itself, without action, unattached, without wanting, at peace. Only through error does it seem caught in worldly life."
verses.notice: Ten qualities of the Self are listed, and then one word explains why we miss them: bhramāt, through error.

words.m: as if caught in worldly life

verses.commentary: The verse is almost a list, and its rhythm is part of its meaning. The Self is the witness, all-pervading, whole, one, free, awareness, without action, unattached, without wanting, at peace. Each word answers a fear the ordinary self lives with. The small self feels incomplete, and the Self is pūrṇa, whole. It feels isolated, and the Self is vibhu, everywhere. It feels busy and pulled, and the Self is akriya and asaṅga, inactive and unattached. Then comes the hinge: bhramāt saṃsāravān iva, through error it seems to be caught in saṃsāra. The word iva, as if, carries the whole argument. In Advaita the Self was never bound and then rescued. The binding is an appearance, like the blue of the sky, which you can see clearly and which is not a property of space. Reading the list slowly, one word per breath, is a traditional way to use a verse like this. Each word is checked against your own experience before moving on.

bridge.note: Krishna names the Supreme Self in the body as the witness, the one who permits and sustains.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: कूटस्थं बोधमद्वैतमात्मानं परिभावय । आभासोऽहं भ्रमं मुक्त्वा भावं बाह्यमथान्तरम् ॥
verses.iast: kūṭasthaṃ bodhamadvaitamātmānaṃ paribhāvaya | ābhāso'haṃ bhramaṃ muktvā bhāvaṃ bāhyamathāntaram ||
verses.en: Meditate on the Self as unchanging awareness, one without a second. Let go of the mistaken idea that you are a reflection, and of every sense of outside and inside.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.13 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "Meditate on the Self as unchanging awareness, one without a second. Let go of the mistaken idea that you are a reflection, and of every sense of outside and inside."
verses.notice: The verse asks you to drop the idea that you are a reflection of awareness.
verses.commentary: Kūṭastha is the anvil in a blacksmith's shop. Everything is hammered on it, and it does not change shape. Ashtavakra uses it for the Self: unchanging awareness, one without a second. The instruction is paribhāvaya, dwell on this repeatedly. Then he names the error to drop: ābhāso 'ham, I am a reflection. Some Advaita schools explain the individual self as awareness reflected in the mind, like the sun reflected in a pot of water. The reflection moves when the water moves, and seems small and shaky. Ashtavakra tells Janaka not to identify with the reflection. Take your stand as the sun instead of its image in the pot. He adds a second thing to drop: the sense of outer and inner. We usually feel that we live inside and the world is outside. If awareness is one without a second, that border is also a construction. This verse is unusual in chapter 1 because it gives a practice, paribhāvaya. Even the Ashtavakra Gita, which later dismisses practice, allows this much: keep returning to what you are.

bridge.note: Krishna describes the imperishable as all-pervading, unthinkable, unchanging, kūṭastha, steady and fixed.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: देहाभिमानपाशेन चिरं बद्धोऽसि पुत्रक । बोधोऽहं ज्ञानखड्गेन तन्निकृत्य सुखी भव ॥
verses.iast: dehābhimānapāśena ciraṃ baddho'si putraka | bodho'haṃ jñānakhaḍgena tannikṛtya sukhī bhava ||
verses.en: My child, you have long been tied by the rope of 'I am the body'. Cut it with the sword of knowing 'I am awareness', and be happy.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.14 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "My child, you have long been tied by the rope of 'I am the body'. Cut it with the sword of knowing 'I am awareness', and be happy."
verses.notice: Ashtavakra calls the king putraka, little son, while handing him a sword.
verses.commentary: The noose in this verse is dehābhimāna, the settled feeling that I am this body. It is old, ciram, and it is tight. Ashtavakra calls Janaka putraka, little son, which is tender and also a little funny given that the speaker is the younger of the two. Then he hands him a sword: the knowledge 'I am awareness'. A sword is used once, cleanly. You do not untie a noose knot by knot when you can cut it. The Advaita teachers read this as the same point made in 1.9 with a fire: knowledge acts all at once, not by degrees. The body still exists and still needs care. What the sword cuts is the identification that makes every ache a threat to me. The sword image also appears in the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna tells Arjuna to cut doubt with the sword of knowledge and stand up. There the result is action. Here the result is happiness. Both are what follows when the noose is gone.

bridge.note: Krishna tells Arjuna to cut the doubt in his heart with the sword of knowledge and stand up.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: निःसङ्गो निष्क्रियोऽसि त्वं स्वप्रकाशो निरञ्जनः । अयमेव हि ते बन्धः समाधिमनुतिष्ठति ॥
verses.iast: niḥsaṅgo niṣkriyo'si tvaṃ svaprakāśo nirañjanaḥ | ayameva hi te bandhaḥ samādhimanutiṣṭhati ||
verses.en: You are unattached and without action, shining by your own light, without stain. This is your bondage: you keep practising samadhi.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.15 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "You are unattached and without action, shining by your own light, without stain. This is your bondage: you keep practising samadhi."
verses.notice: Practising samadhi is named as the bondage itself.
verses.commentary: This is one of the verses that makes the Ashtavakra Gita different from most yoga texts. Samadhi, deep meditative absorption, is usually the goal of practice. Here Ashtavakra says your bondage is that you practise it. The reason is in the first line. You are unattached, actionless, self-luminous and stainless already. If you practise samadhi in order to become free, you have assumed you are not free, and the practice confirms the assumption every day. The commentators read this as a teaching for a particular kind of student, with no contempt for meditation, one like Janaka who is ready to hear the conclusion. For many people, practice is how the mind becomes calm enough to hear this at all, and the Bhagavad Gita says the mind is steadied by practice and dispassion. Ashtavakra is speaking about the last step, where the practitioner sees that the meditator, too, was an idea. The verse is a warning against turning freedom into a project with a finish line.

bridge.note: Krishna tells Arjuna the restless mind is steadied by practice and dispassion, the step this verse assumes is behind you.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: त्वया व्याप्तमिदं विश्वं त्वयि प्रोतं यथार्थतः । शुद्धबुद्धस्वरूपस्त्वं मा गमः क्षुद्रचित्तताम् ॥
verses.iast: tvayā vyāptamidaṃ viśvaṃ tvayi protaṃ yathārthataḥ | śuddhabuddhasvarūpastvaṃ mā gamaḥ kṣudracittatām ||
verses.en: In truth this world is pervaded by you and strung on you. Your nature is pure awareness. Do not fall into smallness of mind.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.16 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "In truth this world is pervaded by you and strung on you. Your nature is pure awareness. Do not fall into smallness of mind."
verses.notice: The world is said to be strung on you, the word used for beads on a thread.
verses.commentary: Prota means strung, as beads are strung on a thread, or woven, as threads run through cloth. Ashtavakra tells Janaka that the world is pervaded by him and strung on him. The thread does not show among the beads, yet nothing holds together without it. Then the verse turns personal: do not fall into kṣudra-cittatā, smallness of mind. The tradition reads this as the practical consequence of the teaching. If the whole world is strung on awareness, then pettiness, grudges and anxious self-concern are a strange way for awareness to behave. It is like a king worrying about a coin. The verse prescribes no effort to become large-minded. It reminds Janaka that he already is, and asks him not to forget it. The same image of beads on a thread appears in the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna says all this is strung on him like pearls on a string. The two texts use one picture for one claim, from two different speakers.

bridge.note: Krishna says all this is strung on him like pearls on a thread.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: निरपेक्षो निर्विकारो निर्भरः शीतलाशयः । अगाधबुद्धिरक्षुब्धो भव चिन्मात्रवासनः ॥
verses.iast: nirapekṣo nirvikāro nirbharaḥ śītalāśayaḥ | agādhabuddhirakṣubdho bhava cinmātravāsanaḥ ||
verses.en: Need nothing, change not, be full and cool at heart, deep in understanding and unshaken. Let your one leaning be toward awareness alone.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.17 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "Need nothing, change not, be full and cool at heart, deep in understanding and unshaken. Let your one leaning be toward awareness alone."
verses.notice: The verse describes a person you could meet: cool, deep, unshaken.

words.m: with your one leaning toward awareness alone

verses.commentary: Most of chapter 1 describes the Self. This verse describes how a person who knows it carries himself. Nirapekṣa means not depending on anything. Nirbhara means full, without hollow places that need filling. Śītalāśaya, cool at heart, is a lovely phrase in a hot country. It means the inner temperature stays even when things heat up. Agādha-buddhi, fathomless understanding, suggests deep water: you cannot touch the bottom with a stick. Akṣubdha, unshaken, is the word for a calm sea. The last phrase is the key to the others. Vāsanā usually means the habit-tendencies that pull the mind back to the same desires. Here Ashtavakra uses it in a good sense: let your one habit be awareness alone. The commentators read this as a concession to how minds work. Minds will lean somewhere, so let them lean toward their source. The portrait resembles the steady-minded person of the Bhagavad Gita's second chapter, who is neither shaken by sorrow nor hungry for pleasure.

bridge.note: Krishna describes the one of steady wisdom, unshaken in sorrow and free of craving in pleasure.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: साकारमनृतं विद्धि निराकारं तु निश्चलम् । एतत्तत्त्वोपदेशेन न पुनर्भवसम्भवः ॥
verses.iast: sākāramanṛtaṃ viddhi nirākāraṃ tu niścalam | etattattvopadeśena na punarbhavasambhavaḥ ||
verses.en: Know that what has form is unreal and what is formless is unmoving. Taught this truth, you do not come back to birth.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.18 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "Know that what has form is unreal and what is formless is unmoving. Taught this truth, you do not come back to birth."
verses.notice: The verse sorts all things into two kinds, with form and without, and says which one is real.

words.m: by teaching on what is real

verses.commentary: Everything with a shape changes. The body grows and ages, mountains wear down, even stars burn out. Ashtavakra says what has form is anṛta, untrue, in the sense that it does not stay what it is. What has no form is niścala, unmoving. The Advaita reading uses a test from the Upanishads: the real is what does not change across past, present and future. By that test, forms fail and awareness passes, since it is present in waking, dream and deep sleep alike. The second line makes a large promise. Through this tattvopadeśa, teaching on what is real, there is no more coming into birth. The commentators explain that rebirth in this tradition follows identification with form. If you take yourself to be the formless, there is nothing to carry from one form to the next. A reader does not need to settle questions about rebirth to use the verse. Its first line is a lens for any loss. What has form was always going to change. What sees the change was never in danger.

bridge.note: Krishna says the unreal has no being and the real never ceases to be.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: यथैवादर्शमध्यस्थे रूपेऽन्तः परितस्तु सः । तथैवाऽस्मिन् शरीरेऽन्तः परितः परमेश्वरः ॥
verses.iast: yathaivādarśamadhyasthe rūpe'ntaḥ paritastu saḥ | tathaivā'smin śarīre'ntaḥ paritaḥ parameśvaraḥ ||
verses.en: As a mirror is present inside the image it holds and all around it, so the Supreme Lord is present inside this body and all around it.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.19 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "As a mirror is present inside the image it holds and all around it, so the Supreme Lord is present inside this body and all around it."
verses.notice: The mirror is both inside the reflection and around it, and so is the Lord with the body.
verses.commentary: Look at a face in a mirror. Where is the mirror? It is behind every point of the image, and it extends past the edges of the image too. The face seems to have depth and to be somewhere, but every part of it is mirror. Ashtavakra says the Supreme Lord is in this body the same way, inside it and all around it. The word chosen is parameśvara, the Supreme Lord, which shows that the Ashtavakra Gita, for all its austerity, does not avoid the language of devotion. The Advaita teachers read the mirror as awareness and the face as the body. The body seems solid and separate, but there is no point in it where awareness is absent, and awareness does not stop at the skin. A practical way to use this verse is to feel the body from inside for a moment, the breath and the weight, and then notice that the knowing of these sensations has no edge. The image is inside the mirror. The mirror is not inside the image.

bridge.note: Krishna says all this is pervaded by him in his unmanifest form, and all beings rest in him.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: एकं सर्वगतं व्योम बहिरन्तर्यथा घटे । नित्यं निरन्तरं ब्रह्म सर्वभूतगणे तथा ॥
verses.iast: ekaṃ sarvagataṃ vyoma bahirantaryathā ghaṭe | nityaṃ nirantaraṃ brahma sarvabhūtagaṇe tathā ||
verses.en: As one all-pervading space is inside a pot and outside it, so Brahman, eternal and unbroken, is in every being.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 1.20 is a verse from chapter 1 (The witness). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "As one all-pervading space is inside a pot and outside it, so Brahman, eternal and unbroken, is in every being."
verses.notice: Break the pot and the space inside does not go anywhere.
verses.commentary: The pot and the space is the second classic example in Advaita, alongside the rope and the snake. A clay pot seems to enclose a little space of its own. But the space inside and outside is one space, and when the pot breaks, nothing moves. The pot-space was never a separate thing. Ashtavakra applies this to Brahman, present in every being. Each body seems to hold a private self, and Brahman is one, eternal and nirantara, without gaps, inside and outside every creature. Chapter 1 ends here, having moved from Janaka's three questions to a picture of the whole of reality. The tradition draws two lessons from the verse. The first concerns death: when the pot breaks, the space is not harmed. The second concerns other people: the space in your pot and the space in your neighbour's pot are the same space. The Bhagavad Gita uses a related image, of the wind that moves everywhere and still rests in space, to say how all beings rest in the Lord.

bridge.note: Krishna compares all beings resting in him to the great wind that moves everywhere and stays within space.

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: अहो निरञ्जनः शान्तो बोधोऽहं प्रकृतेः परः । एतावन्तमहं कालं मोहेनैव विडम्बितः ॥
verses.iast: aho nirañjanaḥ śānto bodho'haṃ prakṛteḥ paraḥ | etāvantamahaṃ kālaṃ mohenaiva viḍambitaḥ ||
verses.en: How strange. I am spotless, at peace, awareness itself, beyond nature. All this time I have been fooled by delusion.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.1 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "How strange. I am spotless, at peace, awareness itself, beyond nature. All this time I have been fooled by delusion."
verses.notice: The student's first words after the teaching are a laugh at himself: all this time.
verses.commentary: Chapter 2 belongs to Janaka. He has heard nineteen verses from his teacher and something has turned over. He begins with aho, an exclamation of wonder that runs through the whole chapter. Then he says what he is: spotless, at peace, awareness, beyond nature. Prakṛti, nature, includes body and mind, so he is placing himself beyond both. The second line has a wry tone. Viḍambita means mocked or made a fool of. For all these years, he says, I have been fooled by delusion. The Advaita tradition values this verse as a picture of what recognition feels like from inside. There is no pride in it and no drama, only surprise that something so plain was missed for so long. Many people know a small version of this, the moment when a family quarrel that felt enormous suddenly looks like a misunderstanding. The rest of chapter 2 is Janaka testing the new view against everything he knows, and finding that it holds.

bridge.note: Arjuna, at the end of the Gita, says his delusion is gone and his memory of who he is has returned.

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: यथा प्रकाशयाम्येको देहमेनं तथा जगत् । अतो मम जगत्सर्वमथवा न च किञ्चन ॥
verses.iast: yathā prakāśayāmyeko dehamenaṃ tathā jagat | ato mama jagatsarvamathavā na ca kiñcana ||
verses.en: As I alone light up this body, so I light up the world. So the whole world is mine, or nothing is.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.2 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "As I alone light up this body, so I light up the world. So the whole world is mine, or nothing is."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: स शरीरमहो विश्वं परित्यज्य मयाधुना । कुतश्चित् कौशलाद् एव परमात्मा विलोक्यते ॥
verses.iast: sa śarīramaho viśvaṃ parityajya mayādhunā | kutaścit kauśalād eva paramātmā vilokyate ||
verses.en: Now that I have let go of the world along with the body, through some skill in the teaching I see the supreme Self.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.3 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "Now that I have let go of the world along with the body, through some skill in the teaching I see the supreme Self."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: यथा न तोयतो भिन्नास्तरङ्गाः फेनबुद्बुदाः । आत्मनो न तथा भिन्नं विश्वमात्मविनिर्गतम् ॥
verses.iast: yathā na toyato bhinnāstaraṅgāḥ phenabudbudāḥ | ātmano na tathā bhinnaṃ viśvamātmavinirgatam ||
verses.en: Waves, foam and bubbles are not different from water. In the same way the world, which comes out of the Self, is not different from the Self.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.4 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "Waves, foam and bubbles are not different from water. In the same way the world, which comes out of the Self, is not different from the Self."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: तन्तुमात्रो भवेद् एव पटो यद्वद् विचारितः । आत्मतन्मात्रमेवेदं तद्वद् विश्वं विचारितम् ॥
verses.iast: tantumātro bhaved eva paṭo yadvad vicāritaḥ | ātmatanmātramevedaṃ tadvad viśvaṃ vicāritam ||
verses.en: Looked at closely, a cloth is only thread. Looked at closely in the same way, this world is only the Self.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.5 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "Looked at closely, a cloth is only thread. Looked at closely in the same way, this world is only the Self."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: यथैवेक्षुरसे क्लृप्ता तेन व्याप्तैव शर्करा । तथा विश्वं मयि क्लृप्तं मया व्याप्तं निरन्तरम् ॥
verses.iast: yathaivekṣurase klṛptā tena vyāptaiva śarkarā | tathā viśvaṃ mayi klṛptaṃ mayā vyāptaṃ nirantaram ||
verses.en: As sugar made from cane juice is filled with that juice, so the world, imagined in me, is filled with me through and through.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.6 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "As sugar made from cane juice is filled with that juice, so the world, imagined in me, is filled with me through and through."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: आत्मज्ञानाज्जगद् भाति आत्मज्ञानान्न भासते । रज्ज्वज्ञानादहिर्भाति तज्ज्ञानाद् भासते न हि ॥
verses.iast: ātmajñānājjagad bhāti ātmajñānānna bhāsate | rajjvajñānādahirbhāti tajjñānād bhāsate na hi ||
verses.en: When the Self is not known, the world appears. When the Self is known, it does not. When the rope is not known, a snake appears. When it is known, the snake is gone.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.7 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "When the Self is not known, the world appears. When the Self is known, it does not. When the rope is not known, a snake appears. When it is known, the snake is gone."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: प्रकाशो मे निजं रूपं नातिरिक्तोऽस्म्यहं ततः । यदा प्रकाशते विश्वं तदाहं भास एव हि ॥
verses.iast: prakāśo me nijaṃ rūpaṃ nātirikto'smyahaṃ tataḥ | yadā prakāśate viśvaṃ tadāhaṃ bhāsa eva hi ||
verses.en: Light is my own form. I am nothing other than that. When the world shines, it is I who shine.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.8 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "Light is my own form. I am nothing other than that. When the world shines, it is I who shine."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: अहो विकल्पितं विश्वमज्ञानान्मयि भासते । रूप्यं शुक्तौ फणी रज्जौ वारि सूर्यकरे यथा ॥
verses.iast: aho vikalpitaṃ viśvamajñānānmayi bhāsate | rūpyaṃ śuktau phaṇī rajjau vāri sūryakare yathā ||
verses.en: How strange. Through not knowing, the imagined world appears in me, like silver in a shell, a snake in a rope, water in the sun's glare.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.9 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "How strange. Through not knowing, the imagined world appears in me, like silver in a shell, a snake in a rope, water in the sun's glare."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: मत्तो विनिर्गतं विश्वं मय्येव लयमेष्यति । मृदि कुम्भो जले वीचिः कनके कटकं यथा ॥
verses.iast: matto vinirgataṃ viśvaṃ mayyeva layameṣyati | mṛdi kumbho jale vīciḥ kanake kaṭakaṃ yathā ||
verses.en: The world came out of me and will dissolve back into me, as a pot into clay, a wave into water, a bracelet into gold.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.10 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "The world came out of me and will dissolve back into me, as a pot into clay, a wave into water, a bracelet into gold."
verses.notice: Three pairs, and each ornament or form dissolves back into what it was made of.
verses.commentary: Janaka gives three examples, each a form and its material. A pot is clay given a shape. A wave is water in motion. A bracelet, kaṭaka, is gold bent into a ring. In each case the form has a name and a use, and in each case it returns to its material without any loss to the material. The clay was never less clay for being a pot. Janaka says the world comes out of him and returns into him in the same way. Advaita uses these examples, which go back to the Chandogya Upanishad's teaching that all clay things are only clay, to explain how one reality can appear as many things. The name and shape are real for use. You drink from the pot and wear the bracelet. But what they are made of is what they are. Applied to the self, the verse removes a fear. If you are the gold, the melting of a bracelet is a change of shape and not an ending.

bridge.note: Krishna says all beings return into his nature at the end of an age and come forth again at its start.

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: अहो अहं नमो मह्यं विनाशो यस्य नास्ति मे । ब्रह्मादिस्तम्बपर्यन्तं जगन्नाशोऽपि तिष्ठतः ॥
verses.iast: aho ahaṃ namo mahyaṃ vināśo yasya nāsti me | brahmādistambaparyantaṃ jagannāśo'pi tiṣṭhataḥ ||
verses.en: How wonderful I am. I bow to myself. I do not perish. Even when the whole world, from Brahma down to a blade of grass, perishes, I remain.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.11 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "How wonderful I am. I bow to myself. I do not perish. Even when the whole world, from Brahma down to a blade of grass, perishes, I remain."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: अहो अहं नमो मह्यमेकोऽहं देहवानपि । क्वचिन्न गन्ता नागन्ता व्याप्य विश्वमवस्थितः ॥
verses.iast: aho ahaṃ namo mahyameko'haṃ dehavānapi | kvacinna gantā nāgantā vyāpya viśvamavasthitaḥ ||
verses.en: How wonderful I am. I bow to myself. Though I have a body, I am one. I go nowhere and come from nowhere. I stand pervading the world.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.12 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "How wonderful I am. I bow to myself. Though I have a body, I am one. I go nowhere and come from nowhere. I stand pervading the world."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: अहो अहं नमो मह्यं दक्षो नास्तीह मत्समः । असंस्पृश्य शरीरेण येन विश्वं चिरं धृतम् ॥
verses.iast: aho ahaṃ namo mahyaṃ dakṣo nāstīha matsamaḥ | asaṃspṛśya śarīreṇa yena viśvaṃ ciraṃ dhṛtam ||
verses.en: How wonderful I am. I bow to myself. No one is as able as I am: without touching it with a body, I have held up this world for all time.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.13 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "How wonderful I am. I bow to myself. No one is as able as I am: without touching it with a body, I have held up this world for all time."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: अहो अहं नमो मह्यं यस्य मे नास्ति किञ्चन । अथवा यस्य मे सर्वं यद् वाङ्मनसगोचरम् ॥
verses.iast: aho ahaṃ namo mahyaṃ yasya me nāsti kiñcana | athavā yasya me sarvaṃ yad vāṅmanasagocaram ||
verses.en: How wonderful I am. I bow to myself. Nothing is mine, or everything that speech and mind can reach is mine.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.14 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "How wonderful I am. I bow to myself. Nothing is mine, or everything that speech and mind can reach is mine."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं तथा ज्ञाता त्रितयं नास्ति वास्तवम् । अज्ञानाद् भाति यत्रेदं सोऽहमस्मि निरञ्जनः ॥
verses.iast: jñānaṃ jñeyaṃ tathā jñātā tritayaṃ nāsti vāstavam | ajñānād bhāti yatredaṃ so'hamasmi nirañjanaḥ ||
verses.en: Knowledge, the known and the knower: these three are not real. I am the spotless one in whom they appear through not knowing.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.15 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "Knowledge, the known and the knower: these three are not real. I am the spotless one in whom they appear through not knowing."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: द्वैतमूलमहो दुःखं नान्यत्तस्याऽस्ति भेषजम् । दृश्यमेतन् मृषा सर्वमेकोऽहं चिद्रसोमलः ॥
verses.iast: dvaitamūlamaho duḥkhaṃ nānyattasyā'sti bheṣajam | dṛśyametan mṛṣā sarvameko'haṃ cidrasomalaḥ ||
verses.en: How strange. Duality is the root of sorrow, and there is no medicine for it except this: all that is seen is unreal, and I am one, pure awareness, without stain.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.16 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "How strange. Duality is the root of sorrow, and there is no medicine for it except this: all that is seen is unreal, and I am one, pure awareness, without stain."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: बोधमात्रोऽहमज्ञानाद् उपाधिः कल्पितो मया । एवं विमृशतो नित्यं निर्विकल्पे स्थितिर्मम ॥
verses.iast: bodhamātro'hamajñānād upādhiḥ kalpito mayā | evaṃ vimṛśato nityaṃ nirvikalpe sthitirmama ||
verses.en: I am awareness alone. Through not knowing, I imagined limits on myself. Reflecting on this always, I rest in what has no divisions.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.17 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "I am awareness alone. Through not knowing, I imagined limits on myself. Reflecting on this always, I rest in what has no divisions."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: न मे बन्धोऽस्ति मोक्षो वा भ्रान्तिः शान्तो निराश्रया । अहो मयि स्थितं विश्वं वस्तुतो न मयि स्थितम् ॥
verses.iast: na me bandho'sti mokṣo vā bhrāntiḥ śānto nirāśrayā | aho mayi sthitaṃ viśvaṃ vastuto na mayi sthitam ||
verses.en: I have no bondage and no freedom. The error has ended, with nothing left to stand on. How strange: the world rests in me, and in truth it does not rest in me.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.18 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "I have no bondage and no freedom. The error has ended, with nothing left to stand on. How strange: the world rests in me, and in truth it does not rest in me."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: सशरीरमिदं विश्वं न किञ्चिदिति निश्चितम् । शुद्धचिन्मात्र आत्मा च तत्कस्मिन् कल्पनाधुना ॥
verses.iast: saśarīramidaṃ viśvaṃ na kiñciditi niścitam | śuddhacinmātra ātmā ca tatkasmin kalpanādhunā ||
verses.en: This world, body and all, is nothing: that is settled. The Self is pure awareness alone. So where could imagining take hold now?
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.19 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "This world, body and all, is nothing: that is settled. The Self is pure awareness alone. So where could imagining take hold now?"

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: शरीरं स्वर्गनरकौ बन्धमोक्षौ भयं तथा । कल्पनामात्रमेवैतत् किं मे कार्यं चिदात्मनः ॥
verses.iast: śarīraṃ svarganarakau bandhamokṣau bhayaṃ tathā | kalpanāmātramevaitat kiṃ me kāryaṃ cidātmanaḥ ||
verses.en: Body, heaven and hell, bondage and freedom, and fear as well: all this is only imagining. What have I, who am awareness, to do with any of it?
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.20 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "Body, heaven and hell, bondage and freedom, and fear as well: all this is only imagining. What have I, who am awareness, to do with any of it?"

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: अहो जनसमूहेऽपि न द्वैतं पश्यतो मम । अरण्यमिव संवृत्तं क्व रतिं करवाण्यहम् ॥
verses.iast: aho janasamūhe'pi na dvaitaṃ paśyato mama | araṇyamiva saṃvṛttaṃ kva ratiṃ karavāṇyaham ||
verses.en: How strange. Even in a crowd I see no second. It has become like a forest to me. What is there to cling to?
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.21 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "How strange. Even in a crowd I see no second. It has become like a forest to me. What is there to cling to?"

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: नाहं देहो न मे देहो जीवो नाहमहं हि चित् । अयमेव हि मे बन्ध आसीद्या जीविते स्पृहा ॥
verses.iast: nāhaṃ deho na me deho jīvo nāhamahaṃ hi cit | ayameva hi me bandha āsīdyā jīvite spṛhā ||
verses.en: I am not the body, and the body is not mine. I am not the separate self. I am awareness. My bondage was this: the craving to keep living.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.22 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "I am not the body, and the body is not mine. I am not the separate self. I am awareness. My bondage was this: the craving to keep living."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: अहो भुवनकल्लोलैर्विचित्रैर्द्राक् समुत्थितम् । मय्यनन्तमहाम्भोधौ चित्तवाते समुद्यते ॥
verses.iast: aho bhuvanakallolairvicitrairdrāk samutthitam | mayyanantamahāmbhodhau cittavāte samudyate ||
verses.en: How strange. In me, the endless ocean, the many waves of the worlds rise at once when the wind of the mind blows.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.23 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "How strange. In me, the endless ocean, the many waves of the worlds rise at once when the wind of the mind blows."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: मय्यनन्तमहाम्भोधौ चित्तवाते प्रशाम्यति । अभाग्याज्जीववणिजो जगत्पोतो विनश्वरः ॥
verses.iast: mayyanantamahāmbhodhau cittavāte praśāmyati | abhāgyājjīvavaṇijo jagatpoto vinaśvaraḥ ||
verses.en: In me, the endless ocean, when the wind of the mind falls still, the ship of the world sinks, by the bad luck of the trader on board, the separate self.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.24 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "In me, the endless ocean, when the wind of the mind falls still, the ship of the world sinks, by the bad luck of the trader on board, the separate self."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: मय्यनन्तमहाम्भोधावाश्चर्यं जीववीचयः । उद्यन्ति घ्नन्ति खेलन्ति प्रविशन्ति स्वभावतः ॥
verses.iast: mayyanantamahāmbhodhāvāścaryaṃ jīvavīcayaḥ | udyanti ghnanti khelanti praviśanti svabhāvataḥ ||
verses.en: How wonderful. In me, the endless ocean, the waves of living beings rise, strike each other, play and sink back, by their own nature.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 2.25 is a verse from chapter 2 (Janaka's wonder). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "How wonderful. In me, the endless ocean, the waves of living beings rise, strike each other, play and sink back, by their own nature."
verses.notice: Living beings are waves that rise, collide, play and sink, by their own nature.
verses.commentary: Chapter 2 ends with the ocean. Janaka sees himself as an endless ocean and living beings as its waves. The four verbs are worth reading slowly: they rise, they strike each other, they play, they sink back. That is a fair summary of any life, and of all lives together. The word ghnanti, they strike or even kill, is not softened. Waves crash into each other. People hurt each other. The verse does not pretend otherwise. What it adds is svabhāvataḥ, by their own nature. The waves do this because that is what waves do, and the ocean is not damaged by any of it. The Advaita reading is that this is how the knower looks at the world, with wonder, āścarya, and without being thrown about. The knower still feels for those who suffer, and sees their suffering from a depth it does not reach. The ocean returns in chapters 6, 7 and 15, each time with a slightly different lesson.

bridge.note: Krishna compares the one at peace to the ocean, which stays still while rivers keep pouring in.

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: अविनाशिनमात्मानमेकं विज्ञाय तत्त्वतः । तवात्मज्ञानस्य धीरस्य कथमर्थार्जने रतिः ॥
verses.iast: avināśinamātmānamekaṃ vijñāya tattvataḥ | tavātmajñānasya dhīrasya kathamarthārjane ratiḥ ||
verses.en: You have known the Self as one and indestructible, as it is. You know the Self and you are steady. How can you still take pleasure in piling up wealth?
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 3.1 is a verse from chapter 3 (The test). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "You have known the Self as one and indestructible, as it is. You know the Self and you are steady. How can you still take pleasure in piling up wealth?"

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: आत्माज्ञानादहो प्रीतिर्विषयभ्रमगोचरे । शुक्तेरज्ञानतो लोभो यथा रजतविभ्रमे ॥
verses.iast: ātmājñānādaho prītirviṣayabhramagocare | śukterajñānato lobho yathā rajatavibhrame ||
verses.en: How strange. Love for objects, which are a mistake, comes from not knowing the Self, as greed for silver springs up when a shell is not known for a shell.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 3.2 is a verse from chapter 3 (The test). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "How strange. Love for objects, which are a mistake, comes from not knowing the Self, as greed for silver springs up when a shell is not known for a shell."

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: विश्वं स्फुरति यत्रेदं तरङ्गा इव सागरे । सोऽहमस्मीति विज्ञाय किं दीन इव धावसि ॥
verses.iast: viśvaṃ sphurati yatredaṃ taraṅgā iva sāgare | so'hamasmīti vijñāya kiṃ dīna iva dhāvasi ||
verses.en: You have known 'I am that in which the world rises like waves in the sea'. Why do you run about like someone poor?
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 3.3 is a verse from chapter 3 (The test). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "You have known 'I am that in which the world rises like waves in the sea'. Why do you run about like someone poor?"

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: श्रुत्वापि शुद्धचैतन्य आत्मानमतिसुन्दरम् । उपस्थेऽत्यन्तसंसक्तो मालिन्यमधिगच्छति ॥
verses.iast: śrutvāpi śuddhacaitanya ātmānamatisundaram | upasthe'tyantasaṃsakto mālinyamadhigacchati ||
verses.en: Even after hearing that the Self is pure awareness and lovely beyond words, a person gripped by sexual craving grows clouded.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 3.4 is a verse from chapter 3 (The test). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "Even after hearing that the Self is pure awareness and lovely beyond words, a person gripped by sexual craving grows clouded."

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: सर्वभूतेषु चात्मानं सर्वभूतानि चात्मनि । मुनेर्जानत आश्चर्यं ममत्वमनुवर्तते ॥
verses.iast: sarvabhūteṣu cātmānaṃ sarvabhūtāni cātmani | munerjānata āścaryaṃ mamatvamanuvartate ||
verses.en: The sage knows the Self in every being and every being in the Self. It is strange that the sense of 'mine' still goes on in him.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 3.5 is a verse from chapter 3 (The test). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "The sage knows the Self in every being and every being in the Self. It is strange that the sense of 'mine' still goes on in him."

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: आस्थितः परमाद्वैतं मोक्षार्थेऽपि व्यवस्थितः । आश्चर्यं कामवशगो विकलः केलिशिक्षया ॥
verses.iast: āsthitaḥ paramādvaitaṃ mokṣārthe'pi vyavasthitaḥ | āścaryaṃ kāmavaśago vikalaḥ keliśikṣayā ||
verses.en: Settled in the highest non-duality and set on freedom, he still falls under desire and is shaken by old habits of pleasure. That is strange.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 3.6 is a verse from chapter 3 (The test). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "Settled in the highest non-duality and set on freedom, he still falls under desire and is shaken by old habits of pleasure. That is strange."

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: उद्भूतं ज्ञानदुर्मित्रमवधार्यातिदुर्बलः । आश्चर्यं काममाकाङ्क्षेत् कालमन्तमनुश्रितः ॥
verses.iast: udbhūtaṃ jñānadurmitramavadhāryātidurbalaḥ | āścaryaṃ kāmamākāṅkṣet kālamantamanuśritaḥ ||
verses.en: He knows desire is the enemy of knowledge, he is weak, his last days are near, and still he longs for pleasure. That is strange.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 3.7 is a verse from chapter 3 (The test). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "He knows desire is the enemy of knowledge, he is weak, his last days are near, and still he longs for pleasure. That is strange."

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: इहामुत्र विरक्तस्य नित्यानित्यविवेकिनः । आश्चर्यं मोक्षकामस्य मोक्षाद् एव विभीषिका ॥
verses.iast: ihāmutra viraktasya nityānityavivekinaḥ | āścaryaṃ mokṣakāmasya mokṣād eva vibhīṣikā ||
verses.en: He has turned from this world and the next, he can tell the lasting from the passing, he wants freedom, and yet he is afraid of freedom itself. That is strange.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 3.8 is a verse from chapter 3 (The test). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "He has turned from this world and the next, he can tell the lasting from the passing, he wants freedom, and yet he is afraid of freedom itself. That is strange."

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: धीरस्तु भोज्यमानोऽपि पीड्यमानोऽपि सर्वदा । आत्मानं केवलं पश्यन् न तुष्यति न कुप्यति ॥
verses.iast: dhīrastu bhojyamāno'pi pīḍyamāno'pi sarvadā | ātmānaṃ kevalaṃ paśyan na tuṣyati na kupyati ||
verses.en: Whether fed with pleasures or tormented, the steady one sees only the Self and is neither pleased nor angry.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 3.9 is a verse from chapter 3 (The test). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "Whether fed with pleasures or tormented, the steady one sees only the Self and is neither pleased nor angry."

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: चेष्टमानं शरीरं स्वं पश्यत्यन्यशरीरवत् । संस्तवे चापि निन्दायां कथं क्षुभ्येत् महाशयः ॥
verses.iast: ceṣṭamānaṃ śarīraṃ svaṃ paśyatyanyaśarīravat | saṃstave cāpi nindāyāṃ kathaṃ kṣubhyet mahāśayaḥ ||
verses.en: He watches his own body acting as if it were someone else's. Praised or blamed, how could such a large-hearted person be shaken?
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 3.10 is a verse from chapter 3 (The test). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "He watches his own body acting as if it were someone else's. Praised or blamed, how could such a large-hearted person be shaken?"

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: मायामात्रमिदं विश्वं पश्यन् विगतकौतुकः । अपि सन्निहिते मृत्यौ कथं त्रस्यति धीरधीः ॥
verses.iast: māyāmātramidaṃ viśvaṃ paśyan vigatakautukaḥ | api sannihite mṛtyau kathaṃ trasyati dhīradhīḥ ||
verses.en: He sees this world as mere appearance and has lost all curiosity about it. How could the steady one be afraid, even when death is close?
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 3.11 is a verse from chapter 3 (The test). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "He sees this world as mere appearance and has lost all curiosity about it. How could the steady one be afraid, even when death is close?"

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: निःस्पृहं मानसं यस्य नैराश्येऽपि महात्मनः । तस्यात्मज्ञानतृप्तस्य तुलना केन जायते ॥
verses.iast: niḥspṛhaṃ mānasaṃ yasya nairāśye'pi mahātmanaḥ | tasyātmajñānatṛptasya tulanā kena jāyate ||
verses.en: The great one's mind wants nothing, even when nothing is left to hope for. Content in knowing the Self, with whom can he be compared?
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 3.12 is a verse from chapter 3 (The test). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "The great one's mind wants nothing, even when nothing is left to hope for. Content in knowing the Self, with whom can he be compared?"

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: स्वभावाद् एव जानानो दृश्यमेतन्न किञ्चन । इदं ग्राह्यमिदं त्याज्यं स किं पश्यति धीरधीः ॥
verses.iast: svabhāvād eva jānāno dṛśyametanna kiñcana | idaṃ grāhyamidaṃ tyājyaṃ sa kiṃ paśyati dhīradhīḥ ||
verses.en: Knowing by nature that what is seen is nothing, how would the steady one look at things as 'this to take' and 'this to throw away'?
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 3.13 is a verse from chapter 3 (The test). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "Knowing by nature that what is seen is nothing, how would the steady one look at things as 'this to take' and 'this to throw away'?"

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: अन्तस्त्यक्तकषायस्य निर्द्वन्द्वस्य निराशिषः । यदृच्छयागतो भोगो न दुःखाय न तुष्टये ॥
verses.iast: antastyaktakaṣāyasya nirdvandvasya nirāśiṣaḥ | yadṛcchayāgato bhogo na duḥkhāya na tuṣṭaye ||
verses.en: For one who has dropped inner impurities, who is free of opposites and of wishes, a pleasure that comes on its own brings neither pain nor delight.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 3.14 is a verse from chapter 3 (The test). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "For one who has dropped inner impurities, who is free of opposites and of wishes, a pleasure that comes on its own brings neither pain nor delight."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: हन्तात्मज्ञानस्य धीरस्य खेलतो भोगलीलया । न हि संसारवाहीकैर्मूढैः सह समानता ॥
verses.iast: hantātmajñānasya dhīrasya khelato bhogalīlayā | na hi saṃsāravāhīkairmūḍhaiḥ saha samānatā ||
verses.en: The steady one who knows the Self plays the game of experience. He has nothing in common with the confused, who carry the world like beasts of burden.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 4.1 is a verse from chapter 4 (The knower at play). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "The steady one who knows the Self plays the game of experience. He has nothing in common with the confused, who carry the world like beasts of burden."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: यत् पदं प्रेप्सवो दीनाः शक्राद्याः सर्वदेवताः । अहो तत्र स्थितो योगी न हर्षमुपगच्छति ॥
verses.iast: yat padaṃ prepsavo dīnāḥ śakrādyāḥ sarvadevatāḥ | aho tatra sthito yogī na harṣamupagacchati ||
verses.en: The state that Indra and all the gods long for, poor in their longing: the yogi stands there and does not grow excited.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 4.2 is a verse from chapter 4 (The knower at play). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "The state that Indra and all the gods long for, poor in their longing: the yogi stands there and does not grow excited."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: तज्ज्ञस्य पुण्यपापाभ्यां स्पर्शो ह्यन्तर्न जायते । न ह्याकाशस्य धूमेन दृश्यमानापि सङ्गतिः ॥
verses.iast: tajjñasya puṇyapāpābhyāṃ sparśo hyantarna jāyate | na hyākāśasya dhūmena dṛśyamānāpi saṅgatiḥ ||
verses.en: Inwardly, one who knows That is not touched by merit or sin, as space is not touched by smoke, though smoke seems to fill it.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 4.3 is a verse from chapter 4 (The knower at play). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "Inwardly, one who knows That is not touched by merit or sin, as space is not touched by smoke, though smoke seems to fill it."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: आत्मैवेदं जगत्सर्वं ज्ञातं येन महात्मना । यदृच्छया वर्तमानं तं निषेद्धुं क्षमेत कः ॥
verses.iast: ātmaivedaṃ jagatsarvaṃ jñātaṃ yena mahātmanā | yadṛcchayā vartamānaṃ taṃ niṣeddhuṃ kṣameta kaḥ ||
verses.en: The great one has known this whole world as the Self. He lives as things come. Who could stop him?
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 4.4 is a verse from chapter 4 (The knower at play). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "The great one has known this whole world as the Self. He lives as things come. Who could stop him?"

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: आब्रह्मस्तम्बपर्यन्ते भूतग्रामे चतुर्विधे । विज्ञस्यैव हि सामर्थ्यमिच्छानिच्छाविवर्जने ॥
verses.iast: ābrahmastambaparyante bhūtagrāme caturvidhe | vijñasyaiva hi sāmarthyamicchānicchāvivarjane ||
verses.en: Among the four kinds of beings, from Brahma down to a clump of grass, only the wise have the strength to give up both wanting and not wanting.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 4.5 is a verse from chapter 4 (The knower at play). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "Among the four kinds of beings, from Brahma down to a clump of grass, only the wise have the strength to give up both wanting and not wanting."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: आत्मानमद्वयं कश्चिज्जानाति जगदीश्वरम् । यद् वेत्ति तत्स कुरुते न भयं तस्य कुत्रचित् ॥
verses.iast: ātmānamadvayaṃ kaścijjānāti jagadīśvaram | yad vetti tatsa kurute na bhayaṃ tasya kutracit ||
verses.en: Rare is the one who knows the Self as one without a second, the Lord of the world. He does what he knows, and has no fear from anywhere.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 4.6 is a verse from chapter 4 (The knower at play). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "Rare is the one who knows the Self as one without a second, the Lord of the world. He does what he knows, and has no fear from anywhere."

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: न ते सङ्गोऽस्ति केनापि किं शुद्धस्त्यक्तुमिच्छसि । सङ्घातविलयं कुर्वन्नेवमेव लयं व्रज ॥
verses.iast: na te saṅgo'sti kenāpi kiṃ śuddhastyaktumicchasi | saṅghātavilayaṃ kurvannevameva layaṃ vraja ||
verses.en: You are tied to nothing. You are pure. What would you give up? Let this bundle of body and mind dissolve, and so go to rest.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 5.1 is a verse from chapter 5 (Four ways to rest). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "You are tied to nothing. You are pure. What would you give up? Let this bundle of body and mind dissolve, and so go to rest."

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: उदेति भवतो विश्वं वारिधेरिव बुद्बुदः । इति ज्ञात्वैकमात्मानमेवमेव लयं व्रज ॥
verses.iast: udeti bhavato viśvaṃ vāridheriva budbudaḥ | iti jñātvaikamātmānamevameva layaṃ vraja ||
verses.en: The world rises from you like a bubble from the sea. Know the Self as one, and so go to rest.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 5.2 is a verse from chapter 5 (Four ways to rest). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "The world rises from you like a bubble from the sea. Know the Self as one, and so go to rest."

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: प्रत्यक्षमप्यवस्तुत्वाद् विश्वं नास्त्यमले त्वयि । रज्जुसर्प इव व्यक्तमेवमेव लयं व्रज ॥
verses.iast: pratyakṣamapyavastutvād viśvaṃ nāstyamale tvayi | rajjusarpa iva vyaktamevameva layaṃ vraja ||
verses.en: Though seen, the world is unreal, and it does not exist in you, the spotless one: it is like the snake in the rope. Know this, and so go to rest.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 5.3 is a verse from chapter 5 (Four ways to rest). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "Though seen, the world is unreal, and it does not exist in you, the spotless one: it is like the snake in the rope. Know this, and so go to rest."

verses.speaker: ashtavakra
verses.sa: समदुःखसुखः पूर्ण आशानैराश्ययोः समः । समजीवितमृत्युः सन्नेवमेव लयं व्रज ॥
verses.iast: samaduḥkhasukhaḥ pūrṇa āśānairāśyayoḥ samaḥ | samajīvitamṛtyuḥ sannevameva layaṃ vraja ||
verses.en: The same in pain and pleasure, full, the same in hope and disappointment, the same in life and death: being so, go to rest.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 5.4 is a verse from chapter 5 (Four ways to rest). The sage Ashtavakra speaks it to King Janaka. In plain English it says: "The same in pain and pleasure, full, the same in hope and disappointment, the same in life and death: being so, go to rest."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: आकाशवदनन्तोऽहं घटवत् प्राकृतं जगत् । इति ज्ञानं तथैतस्य न त्यागो न ग्रहो लयः ॥
verses.iast: ākāśavadananto'haṃ ghaṭavat prākṛtaṃ jagat | iti jñānaṃ tathaitasya na tyāgo na graho layaḥ ||
verses.en: I am endless like space. The world of nature is like a pot. Knowing this, there is nothing to give up, nothing to take and nothing to dissolve.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 6.1 is a verse from chapter 6 (Space, ocean, shell). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "I am endless like space. The world of nature is like a pot. Knowing this, there is nothing to give up, nothing to take and nothing to dissolve."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: महोदधिरिवाहं स प्रपञ्चो वीचिसन्निभः । इति ज्ञानं तथैतस्य न त्यागो न ग्रहो लयः ॥
verses.iast: mahodadhirivāhaṃ sa prapañco vīcisannibhaḥ | iti jñānaṃ tathaitasya na tyāgo na graho layaḥ ||
verses.en: I am like the great ocean. The world of many things is like a wave. Knowing this, there is nothing to give up, nothing to take and nothing to dissolve.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 6.2 is a verse from chapter 6 (Space, ocean, shell). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "I am like the great ocean. The world of many things is like a wave. Knowing this, there is nothing to give up, nothing to take and nothing to dissolve."
verses.notice: The same refrain closes all four verses of chapter 6: nothing to give up, take or dissolve.

words.m: the spread-out world of many things

verses.commentary: In chapter 5 Ashtavakra told Janaka four times to go to rest, layaṃ vraja, to dissolve. In chapter 6 the reply, in four verses, is that there is nothing to dissolve. This verse gives the ocean image. I am like the great ocean, and the world of many things is like a wave. Knowing this, there is no giving up, no taking and no dissolving. The refrain is the point. If the wave is water, you do not need to throw it away to reach the water, and you do not need to grab it either. Even dissolving it is unnecessary, since it is already nothing other than ocean. The Advaita teachers see chapter 6 as a refinement. Renunciation and absorption are useful ideas on the way, but they still assume a world standing apart from the Self. Once that assumption is gone, these efforts have no object. For a reader, the verse is an invitation to stop managing. Some days the waves are high. You are still the ocean.

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: अहं स शुक्तिसङ्काशो रूप्यवद् विश्वकल्पना । इति ज्ञानं तथैतस्य न त्यागो न ग्रहो लयः ॥
verses.iast: ahaṃ sa śuktisaṅkāśo rūpyavad viśvakalpanā | iti jñānaṃ tathaitasya na tyāgo na graho layaḥ ||
verses.en: I am like the shell. The world is imagined, like the silver. Knowing this, there is nothing to give up, nothing to take and nothing to dissolve.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 6.3 is a verse from chapter 6 (Space, ocean, shell). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "I am like the shell. The world is imagined, like the silver. Knowing this, there is nothing to give up, nothing to take and nothing to dissolve."

verses.speaker: janaka
verses.sa: अहं वा सर्वभूतेषु सर्वभूतान्यथो मयि । इति ज्ञानं तथैतस्य न त्यागो न ग्रहो लयः ॥
verses.iast: ahaṃ vā sarvabhūteṣu sarvabhūtānyatho mayi | iti jñānaṃ tathaitasya na tyāgo na graho layaḥ ||
verses.en: I am in every being, and every being is in me. Knowing this, there is nothing to give up, nothing to take and nothing to dissolve.
verses.quick: Ashtavakra Gita 6.4 is a verse from chapter 6 (Space, ocean, shell). King Janaka speaks it to his teacher, the sage Ashtavakra. In plain English it says: "I am in every being, and every being is in me. Knowing this, there is nothing to give up, nothing to take and nothing to dissolve."
